title: Place Value for Grade 1: Tens and Ones Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Place Value Grade 1: Tens and Ones Made Simple
meta_desc: Teach place value to Grade 1 with tens and ones the easy way — bundling straws, the teen-number trap, expanded form and a free quiz. Try it now.
excerpt: The moment a child sees that 34 is three bundles of ten and four loose ones, two-digit numbers stop being scary. Here is how I teach tens and ones in Grade 1, teen traps and all, with a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 34 on a slate and ask a Grade 1 child what it means, and most will read it as ‘three, four’ — two separate digits sitting side by side. That is the exact gap place value fills. The whole idea of tens and ones in Grade 1 is teaching a child that the 3 in 34 is not a lonely three; it stands for three groups of ten, which is thirty, and the 4 is four loose ones. Get that one idea to land and two-digit numbers stop being a wall.

I teach this with things a child can actually pick up and bundle, not with a printed number line. Straws, matchsticks, ice-cream sticks, even dried rajma beans in little cups. The physical act of tying ten straws into one bundle is what makes the abstract idea click. Below is the order I follow, the teen-number trap that trips up nearly every six-year-old, and how a simple tens-and-ones chart ties it all together.

Start by bundling into groups of ten

Give the child a big pile of straws — say, twenty-six of them — and ask them to count. Watch them count one by one and lose track somewhere around eighteen. That frustration is the teaching moment. Now show them the trick: count out ten straws, wrap a rubber band around them, and set the bundle aside. Do it again. Now you have two bundles and six loose straws.

Ask the question that matters: ‘How many straws altogether?’ Two tens and six ones. Twenty-six. The child has just built the number instead of memorising it. In my experience teaching six-year-olds, this beats any worksheet in the first week — the hands do the understanding before the pencil does.

Bundles are the whole idea

Keep the language consistent every single time: a bundle is a ten, a loose straw is a one. When a child says ‘three bundles and two loose’ and then writes 32, the two-digit number finally has a meaning behind it. Do not rush to the symbol 32 until the bundles feel obvious.

The teen numbers are the tricky part

Here is the honest caveat nobody warns parents about: the teen numbers are backwards, and children are right to be confused. Take 14. We say ‘fourteen’ — the four comes first when we speak, but when we write it, the ten comes first: 1 ten and 4 ones. The word order and the digit order disagree.

Twenty-four does not have this problem — we say ‘twenty’ (the tens) then ‘four’ (the ones), matching how we write it. But fourteen, sixteen, nineteen? The ones are announced first. That is why a child who confidently handles 34 will still write 41 when you say fourteen. It is not carelessness; the language is genuinely misleading.

My fix is to always build teen numbers with straws too. For fourteen: one bundle, four loose. Say it slowly — ‘one ten and four ones’ — before saying ‘fourteen’. Doing the maths order first, then the spoken word, retrains the ear.

Expanded form: 34 is 30 + 4

Once bundles are secure, expanded form is a small, satisfying step. It simply writes down what the bundles already show. Thirty-four is three tens and four ones, which is 30 + 4. Forty-seven is 40 + 7. The child pulls the number apart into the tens part and the ones part, and the plus sign glues them back.

This is worth practising both directions. Give them 50 + 8 and ask for the number (58). Give them 63 and ask them to break it up (60 + 3). That back-and-forth is where place value turns from a party trick into something they own.

The tens-and-ones chart pulls it together

A tens-and-ones chart is just two columns: Tens on the left, Ones on the right. It mirrors exactly how we write numbers, which is the point. The child drops their bundle count in the Tens column and their loose count in the Ones column, then reads the two digits together.

NumberTensOnesExpanded form
262620 + 6
343430 + 4
141410 + 4
505050 + 0
474740 + 7

Notice 50 in that chart. A zero in the ones column is a lovely test — it means five full bundles and not a single loose straw. Children who only ever meet ‘busy’ numbers get thrown by the tidy ones, so put a few in on purpose.

A simple weekly routine that works

Ten minutes a day is plenty at this age. Here is a pattern parents in Tier-2 cities have told me works with almost no prep:

  • Monday and Tuesday: bundle straws for a number you call out — keep the pile under 40.
  • Wednesday: teen-number day. Build 11 to 19 with bundles and say each one ‘ten and __’ before the real word.
  • Thursday: fill in a tens-and-ones chart for five numbers.
  • Friday: expanded form both ways — number to 30 + 4, and 30 + 4 back to the number.
  • Weekend: a mixed printable worksheet so the child has to choose, not be told.

One counter-intuitive thing I have learned: do not correct a wrong teen number by just saying the answer. Hand them the straws and let the bundle show them. A child who fixes their own 41-should-be-14 with a rubber band remembers it far longer than one who is simply told.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz covering exactly what we walked through — counting tens and ones, the teen-number trap, expanded form and reading a chart. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable place value worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Place Value Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on tens and ones, teen numbers and expanded form. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 place value: tens and ones

questions.q: How many tens are in the number 34?
questions.explanation: The first digit shows the tens. In 34, the 3 means three tens, or thirty. The 4 is the ones.

questions.q: How many ones are in the number 26?
questions.explanation: The second digit shows the ones. In 26, the 6 loose ones sit in the ones place; the 2 stands for two tens.

questions.q: What is the expanded form of 47?
questions.explanation: 47 is four tens and seven ones, so it breaks into 40 + 7.
Fourteen sounds like four first, but it is written as 1 ten and 4 ones. That is the teen-number trap.

questions.q: Which number has 5 tens and 0 ones?
questions.explanation: Five full bundles of ten and no loose ones make 50. The zero in the ones place shows nothing is left over.

questions.q: 30 + 6 is the same as which number?
questions.explanation: Three tens is 30 and six ones is 6, so 30 + 6 joins back into 36.

questions.q: A child has 3 bundles of ten straws and 2 loose straws. How many straws?
questions.explanation: Three tens make thirty, plus two loose ones, gives 32.

questions.q: How many tens are in the number 50?
questions.explanation: 50 is five tens and zero ones, so there are 5 tens.

faq.q: At what age should a child understand tens and ones?
faq.a: Most children meet place value in Grade 1, around age six. By the end of the year the aim is to read any two-digit number as a count of tens and ones — for example, seeing 34 as three tens and four ones rather than the digits three and four.

faq.q: Why do teen numbers confuse Grade 1 children?
faq.a: Because the word order is backwards. We say ‘fourteen’ with the four first, but we write it as 1 ten and 4 ones. Building teen numbers with straw bundles and saying ‘one ten and four ones’ before the real word fixes this faster than correction alone.

faq.q: What is the best hands-on way to teach place value?
faq.a: Bundling. Give the child loose straws or matchsticks and have them tie groups of ten together. The physical act of making a bundle is what turns an abstract ten into something concrete, which is why it beats flashcards at this age.

faq.q: What is expanded form and should Grade 1 learn it?
faq.a: Expanded form writes a number as its tens plus its ones — 34 becomes 30 + 4. Yes, it belongs in Grade 1 once bundling is secure, because it simply records what the bundles already show and reinforces the two places.
